nature-eecon-216.title: Weak and strong sustainability: can machines replace nature?
nature-eecon-216.text:
Cut down a natural forest and plant a park or farmland in its place. Is that sustainable? Under {{ref:nature-eecon-217}}, it can be, if the new land's value equals the biodiversity lost. Under {{ref:nature-eecon-218}}, it may not be.

These are two opposing approaches from environmental economics. They differ on one question: can {{ref:nature-found-010}} be replaced by human-made capital? The weak view treats natural and {{ref:nature-econ-531}} as interchangeable. Losing natural capital is acceptable as long as human capital rises by at least as much. The strong view holds that some natural assets have critical ecological functions that no human-made alternative can replace. Those must be kept, whatever the gains elsewhere.

Pearce, Markandya and Barbier's Blueprint for a Green Economy (1989) was among the first works to discuss the ideas. Since the 1990s, economists have argued heatedly over how far the two kinds of capital can substitute for each other, and they still dispute it. Wilfred Beckerman rejects both camps. He calls the weak view "redundant and illogical" and the strong view a "morally repugnant and totally impracticable objective".

nature-eecon-210.title: Environment, society, economy: the three dimensions of sustainability
nature-eecon-210.text: Most writing on {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} splits it into three areas: environmental, social and economic. Writers call them pillars, components, aspects or goals; all mean the same thing here. The familiar diagram of three overlapping circles first appeared in a 1987 article by the economist Edward Barbier. {{ref:nature-gov-127}} (1992) and Agenda 2030 (2015) both frame sustainability through these three dimensions. Yet for all its dominance, the paradigm has few theoretical foundations.

nature-eecon-227.title: Elasticity of substitution: how easily one input replaces another
nature-eecon-227.text: If capital gets cheaper relative to labor, how much more capital will firms use? The elasticity of substitution answers that. It measures the percentage change in the ratio of two inputs used for a percentage change in their relative prices or marginal values. Its most common use is capital against labor. Geometrically, it measures the curvature of an {{ref:nature-econ-308}}: the larger it is, the more readily one input stands in for another. Below one, goods are gross complements, and relative spending on a good rises with its relative price. Above one, they are gross substitutes, and it falls. At exactly one, the Cobb–Douglas case, relative spending ignores relative prices. John Hicks introduced it in 1932, and Joan Robinson independently discovered it in 1933.

nature-eecon-225.title: The Cobb–Douglas production function
nature-eecon-225.text: Between 1927 and 1947, Charles Cobb and Paul Douglas developed and tested a formula linking amounts of labor and capital to output. Their Cobb–Douglas production function is now widely used. In its common form, exponents α and β, each between 0 and 1, are the labor and capital elasticities of output. With α = 0.45, 1% more labor gives about 0.45% more output. It obeys diminishing returns: each extra unit of a factor adds output, but less and less. Its {{ref:nature-eecon-227}} is constant and equal to 1. If the exponents sum to 1, returns to scale are constant; below 1 they decrease, above 1 they increase. It is a limiting case of the {{ref:nature-eecon-226}} function. Critics fault its lack of foundation and its assumption of a constant labor share of output, a share now widely seen to be declining.

nature-eecon-226.title: Constant elasticity of substitution: one formula, many shapes
nature-eecon-226.text: Constant elasticity of substitution (CES) functions keep the ease of swapping one input or good for another the same at all levels of output or utility. Solow introduced the two-factor capital-labor version, popularized by Arrow, Chenery, Minhas and Solow. Linear functions (perfect substitutes), Cobb–Douglas and Leontief functions (perfect complements) are all special cases. With more than two factors, Uzawa showed, it generally cannot keep the elasticity constant between every pair. Modelers therefore nest CES functions, giving each nest its own elasticity. As a utility function, goods become perfect substitutes as the elasticity approaches infinity and perfect complements as it approaches zero.

nature-eecon-212.title: The economic dimension of sustainability
nature-eecon-212.text: The economic dimension asks how economic development fits with protecting the environment and meeting basic needs. It is controversial, because "development" can be read as mere {{ref:nature-econ-478}}, which can promote a system bad for the environment. Yet development can reduce hunger and energy poverty, which is why SDG 8 calls for growth, measured partly by real GDP per person. The Brundtland Report holds that poverty both causes and results from environmental problems. Sources still disagree whether growth belongs in sustainability or undermines it.

nature-eecon-211.title: The nested model: economy inside society, society inside nature
nature-eecon-211.text: The nested model ranks the {{ref:nature-eecon-210}}. It draws the economy inside society, and society inside the environment. Many publications treat the environmental dimension, planetary integrity, as the most important, so it sets limits on economic and social development. The SDG "wedding cake" model shows the same nesting, with the biosphere at the base. A 2022 assessment argued that the SDGs still fail to make protecting planetary integrity an end in itself.

nature-eecon-213.title: Sustainability barriers: why it is so hard
nature-eecon-213.text: Why is sustainability so hard to achieve? Some barriers are intrinsic, rooted in nature's complexity and the human condition. One is the value-action gap: people do not act on their convictions. Other barriers are extrinsic and can be overcome, for example by putting a price on the consumption of public goods. Competitive market economies carry a structural imperative to grow, which blocks change. And political pressure favors the short term over the long.

nature-eecon-214.title: Sustainability transition: changing the whole system
nature-eecon-214.text: A sustainability transition, or transformation, is a deep change across technology, economy, society, values and goals. It must happen at every scale, from local communities to global institutions. It is politically contested, since stakeholders disagree on goals and methods, and it can challenge existing distributions of power and resources. It may only work if far-reaching lifestyle changes accompany new technology, overcoming the {{ref:nature-eecon-213}}.

nature-eecon-230.title: Can human-made capital replace nature?
nature-eecon-230.text: How far can buildings, machinery and technology replace forests, water and clean air? That question of substitutability is the dividing line in the {{ref:nature-eecon-216}} debate, argued ardently since the 1990s. Robert Solow showed that, given some substitutability, piling up produced capital fast enough can offset a shrinking stock of an exhaustible resource. Solow and Stiglitz both held that across-the-board substitution of man-made for natural capital is a real possibility. Georgescu-Roegen countered that the economic process steadily increases {{ref:nature-eecon-109}}, so such sweeping substitution is untenable. William Rees criticizes mainstream economics for assuming perfect substitutability between manufactured or financial capital and natural capital. The two camps still disagree.

nature-eecon-209.title: Sustainable development: meeting needs now and later
nature-eecon-209.text:
The most widely used definition is a single sentence from the 1987 Brundtland Report, {{ref:nature-hist-004}}. Sustainable development meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own. The report stressed two things: the essential needs of the world's poor, and the limits that technology and social organization place on the environment.

The approach tries to balance economic development, environmental protection and social well-being. Its roots are older than the phrase. They lie in 17th- and 18th-century European ideas of sustainable forest management, such as von Carlowitz's sustained-yield forestry.

The 1992 {{ref:nature-hist-003}} in Rio began the Rio Process, which put sustainable development on the international agenda. In 2015 it became the foundational concept of the 17 {{ref:nature-gov-010}} adopted by all UN members.

Scholars understand it in many ways, and critics attack it from several angles. What, exactly, is to be sustained? Some argue that no use of a {{ref:nature-res-209}} can be sustainable, since any extraction eventually exhausts a finite stock. The debate also assumes that societies manage economic, social and natural capital, which may not substitute for one another and whose use may be irreversible.

nature-eecon-222.title: The Brundtland Commission
nature-eecon-222.text: In 1983 the UN set up the World Commission on Environment and Development, chaired by former Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland. Its task was to unite countries in pursuit of sustainable development. It responded to a collision between globalized economic growth and accelerating ecological damage by redefining economic development as {{ref:nature-eecon-209}}. It dissolved in 1987 after releasing {{ref:nature-hist-004}}. That report popularized the term and gave its most used definition, centered on the global poor and on the limits technology and society place on the environment. Its call for an international meeting led to the 1992 Rio summit and {{ref:nature-gov-127}}. The definition's openness won wide support, but critics called it "self-defeating and compromised rhetoric".

nature-eecon-224.title: Intergenerational equity: fairness to those not yet born
nature-eecon-224.text: Children born in 2020 may face up to seven times as many extreme weather events as people born decades earlier. Intergenerational equity is fairness between generations, including between people alive now and those to come. It applies to {{ref:nature-eecon-209}} and climate change, since depleting natural resources will likely burden the future. The two sustainability camps read it differently. A weak-sustainability view is satisfied if environmental losses are offset by greater economic gains, and some of its adherents discount future outcomes. A strong-sustainability view holds that no economic progress justifies leaving a degraded environment. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy weighed decisions by {{ref:nature-gov-225}}. In 1974 James Tobin applied the idea to endowments: spending must not exceed the after-inflation return.

nature-eecon-215.title: Daly's three rules for sustainability
nature-eecon-215.text: In 1990 {{ref:nature-hist-040}} published three operational rules for sustainable development. Harvest each {{ref:nature-res-212}} no faster than it regenerates.. Match the use of non-renewable resources with equal development of renewable substitutes. Keep waste within the environment's {{ref:nature-found-020}}. Break the rules, and natural capital is used up faster than it can be replenished, which is the mark of an unsustainable situation.

nature-eecon-219.title: The capital approach: what each generation hands on
nature-eecon-219.text: The capital approach judges sustainability by the stock of capital each generation passes on: human, natural and other. Development counts as sustainable when it leaves that stock at least unchanged. The most cited kinds are {{ref:nature-econ-531}}, such as skills and knowledge, and natural capital, such as minerals and water. This gives decision makers a way to test {{ref:nature-eecon-224}}, a fair distribution of assets between generations. Critics note how hard it is to turn the many functions of the natural world into money terms.

nature-eecon-218.title: Strong sustainability: some nature cannot be replaced
nature-eecon-218.text: No factory can stand in for the ozone layer. Strong sustainability holds that natural and human-made capital complement each other but are not interchangeable, so certain natural capital must be preserved. The environment performs functions that humans cannot duplicate: biodiversity, pollination, fertile soils, clean air and water, and climate regulation. The view puts ecological scale ahead of economic gain and treats nature as borrowed, to be passed on intact to the next generation. One version defines hard limits tied to planetary boundaries, giving some environmental changes a value that cannot be traded against money.

nature-eecon-217.title: Weak sustainability: nature can be spent if capital grows
nature-eecon-217.text: Under weak sustainability, degrading the ozone layer, tropical forests or coral reefs could count as sustainable, if financial profits or similar gains offset the loss. The view holds that natural capital may decline as long as human-made capital grows enough to keep the total from falling. It rests on Robert Solow and John Hartwick, who held that human capital can substitute for natural capital. It began in the 1970s as an extension of neoclassical growth theory and entered the mainstream in the 1990s. Critics see flaws. Pearce and Atkinson's measure judged most industrialized countries sustainable, Japan included thanks to its high saving rate. Critics add that it can leave regions exposed to shocks. It may please governments and business, but it does not ensure Earth's ecological integrity.

nature-eecon-223.title: Hartwick's rule: invest the resource rents
nature-eecon-223.text: How can a country live off oil without growing poorer when the oil runs out? Hartwick's rule gives an answer, often summed up as "invest resource rents". A nation must invest all the {{ref:nature-res-218}} it earns from the exhaustible resources it extracts, building produced capital that exactly offsets the resource's decline. Solow (1974) showed this works if produced capital can partly substitute for natural resources. The rule is the main route for putting {{ref:nature-eecon-217}} into governance. Extended to many kinds of capital, the net of investment over disinvestment is called {{ref:nature-eecon-220}}. Ecological economists reject its assumptions. Clive Spash criticized its "self-evident lack of realism": it treats man-made capital as never depreciating, and as substituting for nature rather than complementing it.

nature-eecon-228.title: The overlapping generations model
nature-eecon-228.text: The overlapping generations (OLG) model is a leading framework in macroeconomics in which people live for a finite time, long enough to overlap with other generations. It is the natural tool for studying how resources pass between generations, for example through Social Security. Maurice Allais first formulated it in 1947, Paul Samuelson more rigorously in 1958, and Peter Diamond added production in 1965. Surprisingly, its steady-state equilibrium need not be efficient; in Diamond's version people save more than is socially optimal.

nature-eecon-220.title: Genuine savings: is a nation getting richer or poorer?
nature-eecon-220.text: Genuine savings is a money measure of a nation's net change in produced, natural and human capital. Pearce, Atkinson and Hamilton built it on {{ref:nature-eecon-223}}. Under {{ref:nature-eecon-217}}, governance should keep genuine savings at or above zero. The World Bank and others have estimated it for many countries, and a positive value is linked to possible long-run sustainability.

nature-eecon-221.title: The social bequest: what we leave, not how much
nature-eecon-221.text: The social bequest approach asks which specific rights and opportunities we leave to future generations, rather than how much. It aims to escape a "zero-sum" game in which present gains are automatic losses for the future. Daniel Bromley's rainforest example shows the trap of thinking in amounts: using 25% of what remains at each decision would eventually use up the forest.

nature-eecon-229.title: Critical natural capital: the parts that cannot be replaced
nature-eecon-229.text: Air, water and land perform ecological functions no human-made alternative can replace. That makes them critical natural capital, unlike non-critical capital such as minerals. {{ref:nature-eecon-218}} holds that critical assets must be kept, whatever the gains in other kinds of capital. Adjusted net national income subtracts natural resource depletion, but it does not account for critical natural capital.

openers.strong-and-weak-sustainability: Can a factory make up for a lost forest? That question divides weak sustainability from strong sustainability, two opposing approaches that differ on whether natural capital can be replaced by human-made capital. This chapter starts with the economist's tools for the question, such as the elasticity of substitution, which measures how easily one input can be swapped for another. It then follows sustainable development, the goal of meeting present needs without compromising future generations, from the Brundtland Commission to today's debates. Along the way come the three dimensions of sustainability, environmental, social and economic, and the barriers that make a sustainability transition so hard.

reviews.strong-and-weak-sustainability: Everything in this chapter turns on one number: how easily nature can be swapped for machines, the {{ref:nature-eecon-227}}. Weak sustainability assumes the swap is easy, so Hartwick's rule and genuine savings say a nation is sustainable if it reinvests its resource rents. Strong sustainability says some assets, such as clean air, fertile soils and the ozone layer, are critical natural capital that nothing can replace. Both sides claim to serve intergenerational equity, the fairness that the Brundtland Commission put at the heart of sustainable development. Where they differ is in what one generation owes the next.
